newsitem.title: USA: Clinton decision on Mexico criticized in Congress.
newsitem.headline: Clinton decision on Mexico criticized in Congress.

text.p: President Bill Clinton's decision to certify Mexico as a U.S. partner in the war on drugs drew strong bipartisan criticism in Congress on Friday along with a pledge to try to overturn the action.

"The law requires the president to certify that Mexico has 'cooperated fully with the United States, or taken adequate steps on its own' to combat drug trafficking. I do not see how such an assertion can be made," Sen. Dianne Feinstein said.
"I now intend to work with my colleagues to prepare and submit a resolution to disapprove this decision in the Congress," Feinstein, a California Democrat, said in a statement.

Such a resolution would have to be passed by both the House of Representatives and the Senate and sent to Clinton. If the president vetoed it, as he almost certainly would, it would have to be passed again by a two-thirds majority in order to become effective.

"I believe that a bipartisan majority in Congress will overturn the president's certification of Mexico. I will work to make that happen," Senate Foreign Relations Committee Chairman Jesse Helms, a North Carolina Republican, said.

"Have we received some cooperation from Mexico?" asked Feinstein. "Undoubtedly. President (Ernesto) Zeillo and many others are working with us in good faith. But have we received full cooperation? Not even close," she said.
"We cannot continue to allow the drug cartels to operate out of Mexico with a wink and a nod by the Mexican government," Idaho Republican Sen. Larry Craig said.
New Jersey Democrat Sen. Robert Torricelli said the decision would be difficult to explain to U.S. law enforcement officers. "I genuinely regret this decision," he said.
He said he believed Colombia, which was decertified, made more progress against drugs last year than Mexico.

Feinstein, Craig and Torricelli were among 40 senators who sent a letter to Clinton this week urging him to decertify Mexico. House members, including Democratic Leader Richard Gephardt of Missouri, have also called for decertification because of widespread government corruption.
"Recent events make it clear that certifying Mexico at this time is the wrong message to send to the drug kingpins. It says business as usual can continue," Gephardt said.

Sen. Joseph Biden, a Delaware Democrat, said he was disappointed by Clinton's decision. New Mexico Republican Sen. Pete Domenici said Mexico must prove itself as an ally to avoid decertification next year.
Congressional opposition to Mexico's certification intensified after the arrest last week of Mexico's anti-narcotics chief, Gen. Jesus Gutierrez Rebollo, accused of taking bribes from a drug kingpin.

Critics in Congress said they feared Gutierrez might have passed on sensitive information to drug cartel leaders. They also complained that Mexico refused to honour U.S. extradition requests for cartel leaders and failed to cooperate with U.S. drug agents operating in Mexico.
